narrowest_regime: Full-rank least-squares fit (OLS or WLS, with model-based or sandwich SEs). Edge case outside it: with exact collinearity, software that drops aliased columns in listed order (e.g. pivoted QR) makes order decide which column is dropped.
reason: Permuting the columns of X permutes beta-hat = (X'X)^-1 X'y and the matching rows and columns of (X'X)^-1 (and of any sandwich covariance), so each coefficient, its SE, its t-statistic and its p-value are unchanged. Only sequential (Type I) sums of squares depend on order. A numerical check (statsmodels OLS, 4 predictors reversed) matched to 1e-15 for the coefficient, the classical SE, the HC3 SE and the p-value.
bite_note: Order cannot change any reported quantity in a full-rank fit, so leaving the question out changes nothing. In a rank-deficient design the app should refuse or warn about aliasing instead of relying on order.

failing_part: "best reported as the squared Pearson correlation ... because it penalizes predictions that are systematically too high or too low and so is the conservative choice over 1 − SSE/SST"
narrowest_regime: None as stated. The squared correlation is a valid measure of ranking or linear association, reportable alongside, but it is not the conservative R²; 1 − SSE/SST is the conservative one.
reason: The squared correlation does not change when the predictions are shifted or rescaled, so it does not penalize systematic over- or under-prediction at all. 1 − SSE/SST does. Because r² equals the R² of the best linear recalibration a + b·ŷ, and the raw ŷ is the special case a = 0, b = 1, 1 − SSE/SST ≤ r² always, so r² is the optimistic choice. A check gave r² = 0.40 at shifts of 0, 0.5 and 1.0 while 1 − SSE/SST fell from 0.29 to 0.09 to −0.59. Kvålseth 1985 is cited backwards: it, and the work that cites it (Alexander et al. 2015), recommend 1 − Σ(y−ŷ)²/Σ(y−ȳ)² for accuracy.

citations.cite: Kvålseth TO. Cautionary note about R². Am Stat 1985;39(4):279-285
Alexander DLJ, Tropsha A, Winkler DA. Beware of R2: simple, unambiguous assessment of the prediction accuracy of QSAR and QSPR models. J Chem Inf Model 2015 (PMC4530125)

bite_note: The reported cross-validated R² goes up and hides miscalibration (offset or slope shrinkage of out-of-fold predictions), so researchers may accept or rank models that predict worse in absolute terms.

failing_part: "at least 10 events estimates the C-statistic and the calibration slope precisely enough to be useful"
narrowest_regime: None at 10 events. The cited study puts the minimum at about 100 events, ideally 200 or more.
reason: The cited paper concludes that external validation needs a minimum of 100 events and ideally 200 or more. It reports that small validation samples give biased and highly variable estimates of the C-statistic and the calibration slope. With 10 events, the C-statistic's confidence interval spans roughly ±0.15 and the calibration slope is barely identified, so the citation contradicts the threshold it is offered for. Vergouwe et al. 2005 and Riley et al.'s later sample-size work also point to about 100 events or more.

citations.cite: Collins GS, Ogundimu EO, Altman DG. Sample size considerations for the external validation of a multivariable prognostic model: a resampling study. Stat Med 2016;35(2):214-226. doi:10.1002/sim.6787
Vergouwe Y et al. Substantial effective sample sizes were required for external validation studies of predictive logistic regression models. J Clin Epidemiol 2005;58:475-483

bite_note: Offering a held-out score from 10 events invites researchers to report and trust a C-statistic and calibration slope that are mostly noise. The threshold should be about 100 events, or the score should be refused or shown with wide intervals.

failing_part: "its nutrient coefficient is the standard model's exactly, because the residual and total energy span the same model as the nutrient and total energy"
narrowest_regime: Exact equality holds only when the comparison 'standard' model is the stratum-interacted one, Y ~ N + E + stratum + stratum×E (plus the same other covariates). With equal energy slopes across strata it holds approximately against Y ~ N + E + stratum.
reason: The within-strata residual is r_s = N − a_s − b_s·E, which lies in span{1, N, E, stratum, stratum×E}, not in span{1, N, E}, so the spanning argument fails. By Frisch–Waugh–Lovell, r_s is exactly the residual of N on {1, E, stratum, stratum×E}, so its coefficient equals the nutrient coefficient of the fully stratum-interacted standard model. A simulation with sex-specific nutrient–energy slopes reproduced this to 1e-15: the stratified residual gave 0.0863, Y ~ N + E gave 0.0436, Y ~ N + E + sex gave 0.0856, and Y ~ N + E + sex + sex×E gave 0.0863. Keeping E in the outcome model does nothing to the r_s coefficient, because r_s is already orthogonal to E.

citations.cite: Frisch–Waugh–Lovell theorem (standard regression algebra)

bite_note: If the standard model omits the stratum terms, the stratified residual's coefficient can differ greatly (two-fold in the simulation), so the estimand sentence and any side-by-side comparison would be wrong. If sex is already adjusted, the gap shrinks to the sex×energy term, which was small in the simulation (about 0.14 SE).

narrowest_regime: Any least-squares fit (OLS or WLS with the same X and weights for both parts). The 'mostly the tail' label is a stated convention. It is least stable when the primary coefficient is near zero (the share is a ratio with an uncertain denominator), and the tail part's interval should use a heteroskedasticity-robust SE, because max(y−c,0) is skewed.
reason: β-hat = (X'X)^-1 X'y is linear in y, so the coefficients for min(y,c) and max(y−c,0) add exactly to the primary coefficient. A numerical check matched to machine precision. The split is also interpretable: for an outcome bounded below, E[min(Y,c)] and E[(Y−c)+] are the integrals of the survival function below and above c, so the two parts are the mean shift that comes from changes in the distribution below and above the cut. 'More than half' for 'mostly' is definitional, and requiring the tail part's interval to exclude zero is a reasonable guard.
bite_note: It changes the interpretation sentence: the effect is concentrated above the clinical cut, not in the typical person. The mean coefficient alone cannot show this.

failing_part: "if and only if": the 'only if' direction fails for logistic regression, which the stated regime explicitly includes
narrowest_regime: Sufficient condition, any regression: if missingness is independent of the outcome given the model's predictors (it may depend on the missing values themselves), complete-case estimates are unbiased or consistent under a correctly specified model. It is also necessary for linear and most other models, but not for logistic odds ratios.
reason: White & Carlin 2010 support the 'if' direction. In logistic regression, though, complete-records odds ratios stay asymptotically unbiased when missingness depends on the outcome alone, not jointly on outcome and covariates. This is the case-control sampling argument, set out in Bartlett, Harel & Carpenter 2015. A simulation with n = 200,000 and missingness 60% vs 10% by Y alone recovered the exposure log-OR of 0.70 and the covariate log-OR of 0.40 (only the intercept shifted), while the same outcome-dependent missingness biased linear coefficients (0.70 → 0.60). So the 'if and only if' biconditional is false for one of the listed model types.

citations.cite: White IR, Carlin JB. Bias and efficiency of multiple imputation compared with complete-case analysis for missing covariate values. Stat Med 2010;29(28):2920-2931
Groenwold RH et al. Missing covariate data in clinical research: when and when not to use the missing-indicator method for analysis. CMAJ 2012;184(11):1265-1269
Bartlett JW, Harel O, Carpenter JR. Asymptotically unbiased estimation of exposure odds ratios in complete records logistic regression. Am J Epidemiol 2015;182(8):730-736

bite_note: For logistic models where covariate missingness depends on the outcome but not on the covariates, the record would wrongly call complete cases biased. That can push a researcher to multiple imputation, which is biased if the data are MNAR in X, and away from a valid complete-case analysis. For linear and Cox models the stated assumption is the right one to show.

narrowest_regime: Best established for logistic and ridge-logistic models (van den Goorbergh 2022). Extended with weaker evidence to ML learners for calibration harm (Carriero 2025); the AUC part for ML learners rests on less direct evidence.
reason: van den Goorbergh et al. found that random undersampling, random oversampling and SMOTE gave poorly calibrated models that overestimated the minority class's probability, with no gain in discrimination. Their conclusion was that outcome imbalance is not a problem in itself. Class weighting was not in their study, but for logistic regression an inverse-prevalence weight is the expected-value equivalent of random oversampling: it shifts the intercept by about log(w), so it overestimates risk in the same way. Carriero et al. 2025 found the same calibration harm across ML learners, not always fixable by recalibration. A decision needing a different trade-off is served by moving the threshold on calibrated risks.

citations.cite: van den Goorbergh R, van Smeden M, Timmerman D, Van Calster B. The harm of class imbalance corrections for risk prediction models: illustration and simulation using logistic regression. JAMIA 2022;29(9):1525-1534

Carriero A, Luijken K, de Hond A, Moons KGM, van Calster B, van Smeden M. The harms of class imbalance corrections for machine learning based prediction models: a simulation study. Stat Med 2025;44(3-4):e10320

bite_note: Defaulting to no correction keeps the predicted risks calibrated. The natural alternative, SMOTE or class weights, would inflate every rare-class risk the researcher reports or thresholds on.

narrowest_regime: Untargeted MS metabolomics with pooled QCs, as an optional quality filter. The 50% cut is Broadhurst et al.'s upper bound on acceptance (a convention), not a derived optimum.
reason: Broadhurst et al. 2018 define D-ratio = s_QC / s_sample × 100% (eq. 3), which is approximately σ_tech/√(σ_bio² + σ_tech²) (eq. 5). They recommend an acceptance criterion of at most < 50%, so removing features at ≥ 50% matches the source. At D = 50% technical variance is 25% of the total, so 'too little biological relative to technical' is the source's convention, not a derived bound. The fold handling is sound: the filter uses no outcome, so taking the study SD from each training fold cannot leak outcome information and keeps the pipeline honest under cross-validation. Freezing the QC SD is consistent because the QC samples are not study rows.

citations.cite: Broadhurst D, Goodacre R, Reinke SN, et al. Guidelines and considerations for the use of system suitability and quality control samples in mass spectrometry assays applied in untargeted clinical metabolomic studies. Metabolomics 2018;14(6):72 (PMC5960010)

bite_note: It decides which metabolite features enter the analysis. Its effect on fitted results is usually modest, because high-D-ratio features are mostly noise.

failing_part: "rows lost × largest SMD ... is an outcome-blind predictor of how far keeping every row would move the exposure's estimate in units of its 95% interval half-width, good enough to band the noticing"
narrowest_regime: None as a calibrated predictor. At most a crude flag that the excluded rows differ in covariate mix, which by itself does not move a correctly specified conditional coefficient.
reason: How far the estimate moves depends on whether the exposure–outcome relation differs in the removed rows. For energy misreporters, the exposure itself is mismeasured there. Covariate imbalance does not drive it, and a correctly specified adjusted model absorbs covariate differences. The target is also scaled by the half-width, which shrinks as 1/√n, while the predictor does not depend on n. In simulation (30 reps each), share 0.2 with SMD 1.0 and no misreporting gave predictor 0.20 and a move of −0.08 half-widths. Misreporting in the excluded rows with SMD ≈ 0 gave predictor 0.006 but moves of −0.56, −1.62 and −3.36 half-widths at n = 500, 5,000 and 20,000, so the predictor ranks these cases backwards. Nine calibration cases cannot validate such a mapping.

citations.cite: Austin PC. Balance diagnostics for comparing the distribution of baseline covariates between treatment groups in propensity-score matched samples. Stat Med 2009;28:3083-3107 (cited only for the SMD definition, which is correct)

bite_note: The band sets the triage disposition: it would tell a researcher that keeping implausible reporters 'doesn't change' the estimate exactly when misreporting shifts it by several interval half-widths, or flag harmless covariate-mix differences as 'act on it'.

failing_part: "In a randomized trial, covariate adjustment only sharpens precision" (fails for odds and hazard ratios); also "matched sets are analyzed within each set" as a rule for any matched design
narrowest_regime: Linear models or risk differences with pre-specified baseline covariates in an RCT. Individually matched case-control studies for the within-set rule. The case-control and observational-wording parts hold as stated.
reason: For non-collapsible measures (odds ratio, hazard ratio), adjusting for a prognostic baseline covariate in an RCT changes the estimand from marginal to conditional and moves the estimate away from the null. It also raises the SE, so 'only sharpens precision' is wrong there, though power usually rises (Robinson & Jewell 1991). A simulation (n = 200,000) gave an unadjusted log-OR of 0.42 (SE 0.0090) against an adjusted 0.60 (SE 0.0108). Within-set (conditional) analysis is the standard for individually matched case-control data, but an unconditional analysis adjusting for the matching factors is also valid (Pearce 2016). Matched cohorts and frequency matching do not need it. 'A case-control sample cannot give prevalence or absolute risk' holds without external sampling fractions or incidence, and 'association' wording for observational studies is a defensible convention.

citations.cite: Robinson LD, Jewell NP. Some surprising results about covariate adjustment in logistic regression models. Int Stat Rev 1991;59:227-240
Pearce N. Analysis of matched case-control studies. BMJ 2016;352:i969
FDA. Adjusting for Covariates in Randomized Clinical Trials for Drugs and Biological Products. Guidance for Industry, 2023

bite_note: In an RCT with a binary or time-to-event outcome, the app would present the adjusted OR or HR as the same quantity as the unadjusted one with a tighter interval, so its estimand sentence and adjusted-vs-unadjusted comparison mislead. For matched cohorts it would push an unnecessary conditional analysis.

failing_part: "bootstrap optimism correction is the recommended default" as a model-agnostic default; it fails for flexible learners such as random forests (and deep boosted trees) that nearly memorize their training rows
narrowest_regime: Regression-type models (logistic, linear, Cox, possibly penalized) at clinical sample sizes. There the Efron–Gong/Harrell optimism bootstrap is efficient and low-bias (Steyerberg et al. 2001), and the claim's ranking holds; 'single split is weakest' holds generally.
reason: Steyerberg et al. 2001 support the ranking for logistic regression. Bootstrapping gave stable, low-bias estimates, split-sample was pessimistic and highly variable, and they recommend bootstrapping. The optimism bootstrap tests each bootstrap model on the original data, about 63% of which it trained on, so for interpolating learners it badly underestimates optimism. In simulation (n = 300, 10 predictors, true AUC from 20,000 test rows), random forests gave true AUC 0.682 and apparent AUC 1.000; the bootstrap-corrected AUC was 0.947 (+0.27 bias), while 5-fold CV repeated twice gave 0.675. Logistic regression gave a bootstrap-corrected bias of only +0.003. Iba et al. 2021 also report inconsistent bootstrap biases at small n.

citations.cite: Steyerberg EW, Harrell FE Jr, et al. Internal validation of predictive models: efficiency of some procedures for logistic regression analysis. J Clin Epidemiol 2001;54(8):774-781

Iba K, Shinozaki T, Maruo K, Noma H. Re-evaluation of the comparative effectiveness of bootstrap-based optimism correction methods in the development of multivariable clinical prediction models. BMC Med Res Methodol 2021;21:9

bite_note: For forest or boosted-tree fits, a seal card that ranks the optimism bootstrap first would report grossly optimistic performance (0.95 against a true 0.68 in the simulation). The ranking should depend on the model family: bootstrap for regression models, repeated CV for tree ensembles.

failing_part: "more than 10 repeating values ... is a unit structure", read as licensing clustered intervals, and the 10 cut itself (FEW_UNITS reuses CATEGORY_LEVELS = 10, a category-count constant with no cluster-inference reason)
narrowest_regime: The direction is right. With fewer than 3 distinct values a column cannot support cluster-robust intervals (G = 2 leaves 1 df), and a few repeating word labels such as Self/Proxy or mother/father are attributes, not units. Treating a column as a clustering unit is safe for intervals only with many clusters (roughly 30–50+), or with small-sample corrections (CR2/Bell–McCaffrey with Satterthwaite df, wild cluster bootstrap).
reason: Cluster-robust intervals are anticonservative with few clusters (Cameron & Miller 2015), so crossing 10 distinct values does not make clustering by the column valid. In a simulation (20 rows per cluster, skewed cluster-level regressor, CR1 with t(G−1)), nominal 95% intervals covered 83% at G = 5, 84% at G = 11 and 86% at G = 20. The 3/10 cut points are a naming and recognizer heuristic, presented with a methods reason (unit structure) they do not have. The word-label exception can also misclassify a small study whose subjects are coded by name.

citations.cite: Cameron AC, Miller DL. A practitioner's guide to cluster-robust inference. J Hum Resour 2015;50(2):317-372
Bell RM, McCaffrey DF. Bias reduction in standard errors for linear regression with multi-stage samples. Survey Methodology 2002;28:169-181

bite_note: Below 3 values, refusing is right. Between 11 and about 30 units, the app would cluster intervals without a small-sample correction and report intervals that are too narrow. Classifying 6–10 named subjects as non-units could also leave repeated measures treated as independent.

failing_part: "is enough to choose settings that predict at least as well as the standard settings" (no such guarantee), and the counts "8 ... 16", which no accuracy argument derives
narrowest_regime: In expectation, and where the defaults are clearly suboptimal, a small Sobol budget plus the defaults, chosen by inner CV, usually matches or beats the defaults. Where the defaults are near-optimal it loses slightly in many individual runs.
reason: Bergstra & Bengio's low-effective-dimension argument shows random search beats grid search for a fixed budget. It says nothing about whether 8 or 16 candidates beat the defaults. Choosing by noisy inner-CV scores can pick a configuration that generalizes worse than the default: Schneider, Bischl & Feurer 2025 find this in about 10% of benchmark cases, especially at small n. A simulation (random forest, n = 300, 8 Sobol candidates over mtry and leaf size plus defaults mtry = 1/3 and leaf = 5, 5-fold inner CV, 30 reps) showed the tuned model beating the defaults in all 30 reps (+0.02 to +0.08 test R²) under a sparse nonlinear signal. Under a dense weak linear signal it was worse in 15 of 30 reps (mean −0.004, worst −0.041).

citations.cite: Bergstra J, Bengio Y. Random search for hyper-parameter optimization. JMLR 2012;13:281-305
Bischl B et al. Hyperparameter optimization: foundations, algorithms, best practices, and open challenges. WIREs Data Min Knowl Discov 2023;13(2):e1484
Schneider L, Bischl B, Feurer M. Overtuning in hyperparameter optimization. arXiv:2506.19540 (2025)

bite_note: The budget decides the fitted settings, and the assurance would be wrong in individual runs where the defaults are near-optimal; the losses are small on average but occasionally about 0.04 R². Fix: keep the defaults unless a candidate beats them by more than the inner-CV noise (a one-SE rule), and drop the 'at least as well' wording.
